limitation.description: No official Go rendezvous behaviour donor is pinned; Go directions remain explicitly limited.
Pinned Rust mDNS lacks the private fingerprinted service configuration.
Pinned Rust Noise and fixed-ALPN TLS paths use fallback post-security mux negotiation, not Go-style inline muxing.

native.description: Production C++23 host over TCP/Yamux and QUIC with autonomous discovery, routing and reachability.

private_network.description: Production TCP/Yamux host with a private-network transport PSK layer; QUIC, Relay and DCUtR are outside this profile.

browser_transport.description: Browser and proxy friendly transports; WebSocket is the first committed delivery.

experimental.description: Optional donor protocols that do not gate the declared native production profile.

legacy.description: Deprecated or insecure donor surfaces that Forge rejects deliberately.

capabilities.rationale: QUIC v1 is a native production transport and remains part of the current implementation inventory.
TCP with Yamux is the interoperable stream transport for native and private-network profiles.
Protocol and security negotiation is shared by every supported libp2p transport profile.
Authenticated peer identity is mandatory before protocol, address or topology facts are trusted.
Echo remains a bounded diagnostic fixture and is not advertised as a production libp2p service.
Ping wire request/response is current Go/Rust-compatible protocol support; periodic RTT sampling and health state are a separate host-local Stage 6 policy.
Bounded periodic Ping scheduling, peer-health aggregation and backoff are Forge host-local liveness policy; the underlying Ping wire protocol remains independently interoperable.
Session-time Identify and full-snapshot Push are required sources of remote protocol and address truth.
Forge Peer Exchange is an explicit product extension whose hints remain untrusted until authenticated connect and Identify.
AutoNAT v1 probe scheduling, confidence and reachability events are Forge host-local policy; the distinct v1 client and service wire roles retain Go/Rust interop gates.
AutoNAT v2 address evidence, confidence and lifecycle are Forge host-local policy; the distinct v2 client and service wire roles retain Go/Rust interop gates.
AutoNAT v1 client negotiation and observation remain a distinct donor-compatible wire gate.
Serving AutoNAT v1 is opt-in and requires independent dial policy, rate limits and abuse bounds.
AutoNAT v2 client nonce/data exchange has its own codec, lifecycle and interop evidence.
Serving AutoNAT v2 is independently configurable and must enforce dial-data and resource limits.
Circuit Relay v2 client transport and reservation wire mechanics are separate from autonomous candidate selection.
AutoRelay owns verified candidate selection, bounded reservations, renewal and replacement over the relay client; its orchestration is host-local rather than a bilateral wire interop claim.
Operating a public relay is opt-in and requires separate ACL, reservation, connection and byte limits with Go/Rust service-client interop.
One node-owned attempt state must coalesce direct upgrades while retaining the working relay fallback.
Amino peer, provider and validated value operations use isolated bounded routing and record state.

Configured rendezvous points are an optional standard discovery source owned by the topology manager. Rust is supported by the pinned donor; Go is explicitly limited because no official Go rendezvous behaviour donor is pinned.
Current meshsub negotiation and delivery remain partial until Stage 6 completes v1.0 fallback, scoring and mesh-repair behavior.
Bounded operational peer state and durable cache hydration are host prerequisites, not DHT routing state.
Bootstrap admission and retry are node-owned and feed normal topology without plugin maintenance loops.
Stage 6 extends the managed topology with local discovery, reachability and path-state inputs.
Session reservations are already tracked and remain part of the broader Stage 6 resource model.
Negotiated stream reservations remain mandatory across success, cancellation and shutdown paths.
Logical dial ownership bounds endpoint and relay fallback attempts as one operation.
Transport-backed byte reservations prevent hidden unbounded queues.
Watermarks, protection and score-aware pruning own connected-peer topology.
Official plugins must expose the same node-owned behavior without creating parallel network loops.
Production diagnostics need bounded host, transport and protocol metrics without using metrics as mutable control state.
Public mDNS is optional zero-configuration LAN discovery with pinned Go and Rust donor behavior.

The libp2p mDNS specification defines the private fingerprinted namespace but not the fingerprint computation. Forge uses the pinned Rust pnet Salsa20/SHAKE128 algorithm and its Go-IPFS golden vector. Go interop explicitly configures the service name; pinned Rust mDNS cannot configure a private service name.

DNSAddr TXT expansion is integrated through node-owned resolution and scheduling, with canonical-root attribution and TCP-only private-network filtering. Current denotes implemented feature ownership, not production readiness: the mapped feature remains unverified until exact-head live Go/Rust evidence passes. Registered native/private scenarios and expected_status are acceptance requirements, not recorded results; they do not establish dual-stack or black-hole interop.
Independent peer observations need activation, expiry and confidence before an external address is advertised; the manager is host-local policy rather than a bilateral wire interop claim.
UPnP is an explicit deploy-time capability whose mappings must renew, expire and feed confirmed external addresses.
Forge defines private-profile Internet egress policy. AutoNAT and UPnP donors inform patterns and limitations, but no libp2p specification defines this host-local Forge policy.
The private profile uses a bilateral Go/Rust transport PSK layer, not a negotiated protocol ID, before ordinary secure-channel negotiation.
Policy needs staged rejection points for peer dial, address dial, accept, secured identity and upgraded connection.
Production limits must account for memory, file descriptors, transient work and per-service resources, not only sessions and streams.

The node-owned scheduler applies bounded donor-style address-family and transport staggering. Native/private real-node dual-stack tests exercise an IPv4 authenticated winner with a stalled IPv6 handshake, one logical reservation and joined loser cleanup; ranker/scheduler tests cover launch ordering and bounds. This is host-local behavior, not a wire protocol. The Stage 6 decision retains pending PR5 promotion ownership; the implemented feature mapping remains unverified pending final-head acceptance.

Node-owned IPv6 detection is retained in native and TCP-only private profiles. Deterministic detector/scheduler tests cover attributable failures, suppression, periodic successful probes, reset and resource release. These are component proofs, not a real-network IPv6 outage or donor wire experiment. The Stage 6 decision retains pending PR5 promotion ownership; the implemented feature mapping remains unverified pending final-head acceptance.

The node-owned scheduler applies UDP detection in the native profile and disables it for TCP-only private nodes. Deterministic detector/scheduler tests cover attributable failures, suppression, periodic successful probes, reset and resource release without sending test traffic to the scripted public addresses. This is host-local policy, not donor wire interoperability. The Stage 6 decision retains pending PR5 promotion ownership; the implemented feature mapping remains unverified pending final-head acceptance.
Typed bounded events are required for address, reachability, connection and path changes without polling diagnostics as control state.
Modern coordinated dial and port reuse are part of direct path establishment; no legacy /libp2p/simultaneous-connect negotiation is permitted.
The deprecated /libp2p/simultaneous-connect protocol is deliberately excluded; modern coordination uses direct dial and port reuse without negotiating that ID.

Inlined muxer negotiation is optional to activate but required Stage 6 support: Go TLS and Noise support inline negotiation, while pinned Rust TLS fixes ALPN and Rust Noise handles extensions before the documented fallback rather than claiming inline support.
IDONTWANT and v1.2 behavior are part of the pinned modern GossipSub donor surface.

v1.3 sends one first-RPC extension advertisement; Go extensions.go and Rust behaviour.rs advertise and handle it, unknown extensions are ignored and capability matching decides use rather than negotiating a separate protocol.
Partial Messages remains opt-in at runtime but is required Stage 6 support with Go/Rust extension interop, not an open-ended non-negotiation decision.
Forge parses ws/wss multiaddrs but intentionally defers P2P dial/listen support to Stage 9.
WebTransport belongs to a later browser transport profile and does not block the native production profile.
WebRTC is tracked as a future browser transport rather than being silently omitted from donor parity.
The active HTTP transport drafts need a separate contract decision and do not alter Forge API-over-P2P support.
Automatic certificate acquisition is classified with the future WSS boundary and is not implied by existing P2P TLS authentication.
Unix-domain transport is host-local and requires an explicit product use case before entering the supported profile.
Fetch is a working draft; Content Swarm uses Forge API streaming unless a later interop requirement selects this protocol.
Request-response is a behavior pattern; Forge applications use raw negotiated streams or Forge API rather than a duplicate P2P abstraction.
The performance protocol is useful for benchmarks but is not a production host capability.
Floodsub is a legacy protocol and is not required when GossipSub is the declared production pubsub profile.
Episub is an experimental pubsub design and does not gate the declared GossipSub production profile.
RED is tracked as experimental donor work rather than being silently treated as part of GossipSub compatibility.
Mplex is retained only as donor history; Yamux is the supported TCP stream multiplexer.
Plaintext cannot satisfy production peer authentication and is limited to explicit protocol fixtures.
SECIO is deprecated and replaced by Noise and TLS.
Circuit Relay v1 is intentionally rejected; the production profile requires Circuit Relay v2.
Canonical multiaddrs and signed peer records are owned by Forge multiformats and identity components and consumed by P2P.
